extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in television/late-night comedy and SNL fans
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and informal standards relevant to creating and evaluating televised sketch comedy (especially live/late-night sketches), including what makes a sketch 'play' in rehearsal, production decisions about cutting/trimming, and performance conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live room reaction / big laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: The sketch "played strongly in the room, drawing big laughs" according to audience members at dress rehearsal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience response in dress rehearsal is treated as a key signal of a sketch's comedic success; strong in-room laughs indicate the joke landings regardless of whether the sketch airs live. Example: the sequel reportedly played strongly in rehearsal even though it was cut before broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viral/shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: The first installment "quickly became one of SNL’s most widely shared sketches of the past several seasons."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sketch's potential to be shared widely online (YouTube, social platforms) is an important measure of impact beyond the live broadcast. Even if a sketch is cut from the live show, its viral potential makes it valuable to produce or to post later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking character (performance convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically a rule at SNL: "it was one of Michaels’ rules: no breaking of character," though some audience/commenters view breaking as funny and now it sometimes happens without repercussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining character has traditionally been a cardinal production rule; breaking character can be seen as an anti-pattern by purists but may also produce audience laughter. Producers must decide whether to enforce no-breaking standards or allow spontaneous breaks when they enhance comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production decisions: trimming/cutting for time or other reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL "frequently posts sketches that are cut after dress rehearsal or trimmed for time to its YouTube channel" and the sequel was "cut before the episode’s live broadcast" for unclear reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches may be removed or shortened for non-quality reasons (time, pacing, running order) even if they tested well in rehearsal. Teams should plan for the possibility of post-production release if a sketch is cut from the live show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heavy makeup/prosthetics and uncanny lookalikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Gosling and Mikey Day appeared "under heavy makeup and prosthetics" as uncanny Beavis and Butt-Head lookalikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformative makeup/prosthetics and uncanny resemblance to known characters can be a central comedic device; production must invest in design, and performance must lean into the visual gag. Risk: heavy makeup may affect movement or timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging recognizable characters/crossovers
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequel added "another animated lookalike...Sarah Sherman appearing as Tina Belcher from Bob’s Burgers," using a recognizable cartoon character to derail the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing in well-known characters or crossovers can amplify jokes by tapping audience familiarity and contrast (e.g., Tina Belcher’s voice/awkwardness derails a TV discussion). Legal/rights and audience recognition considerations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor/moderator as comedic foil
rubrics_metrics.description: The setup involved a NewsNation anchor moderating a panel discussion "when the segment was derailed by two audience members," with anchors "struggling to keep from breaking."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a straight-faced moderator or anchor who attempts (and perhaps fails) to maintain control provides a structure for escalating comedy; the actor's ability to sell exasperation vs break contributes to the sketch's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest-host casting and star power
rubrics_metrics.description: Ryan Gosling returned as a performer in the sketch; guest hosts can play multiple roles (e.g., starring as an audience member lookalike).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting high-profile guest hosts can drive attention and shape sketch choices (viral potential, impersonation gags). Writers/producers should tailor material to the host's range and public persona.
